newsitem.title: USA: Bone-chilling start to U.S. inaugural festivities.
newsitem.headline: Bone-chilling start to U.S. inaugural festivities.

text.p: The 53rd U.S. presidental inaugural festivities began on Saturday in bone-chilling cold that checked the size of crowds attending events on the national Mall, but not their enthusiasm.

President Bill Clinton, who takes the oath of office at noon on Monday, spent his day mixing business with pleasure -- hosting both a brunch and a lunch for about 500 friends from Arkansas and college.
He also worked on yet another draft of his inaugural address, re-writing "a whole new beginning," according to White House spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn.

The official three-day celebration began with "An American Journey" festival on the Mall -- a wide stretch of land that reaches from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial -- and featured a variety of music, food and interactive technology.
Event organisers erected seven "heated" tents that for the most part were only slightly warmer than if you stood outside, mainly because the white canvas at least cut down the wind.
The National Weather Service said temperatures were expected to remain in the teens (-7 to -10 Celsius) for most of the day, and cautioned that wind-chill factors made it feel much worse.
The thousands who bundled up and turned out, however, seemed glad they came.
"This only happens once every four years. We didn't want to miss it," said Tom Wilson of Laurel, Md., who came to the Mall with wife, Chris, and their three small children.

At the tent called "Harmony Hall," a man wearing multiple layers of clothing topped by a white-hooded sweatshirt, picked up a microphone and gazed out at the audience of more than 100 diehards sitting in the metal chairs set up for more than a thousand.
"I don't know what to say," he told the audience, "but on behalf of everyone ... who has been working on this thing, we seriously admire you for coming here and sitting on those chairs."
A U.S. Army brass quintet then came on stage and performed compositions from the 1800s.

At the food tents, with booths featuring such cuisine as jambalaya, fried chicken livers, chicken teriyaki, couscous, and Italian sausage and french fries, workers wearing hoods and earmuffs served their patrons.
The loneliest man at the American Kitchen tent was Drew Shack of Columbia, Md. The lemon ice he was selling was not a hot item.
"It's warmer in my freezer than it is in the tent," he said. "I'm serious. The freezer's set at 32 degrees (0 Celsius). It's 26 (-3 Clesius) in the tent."
"You take it out and it freezes like a rock," he said.
Saturday's public activities were to conclude with a fireworks display, hailed by organisers as one of the most elaborate held in Washington -- but brief, only about 12 minutes in duration.
